title: B2C Mobile App
description: The highest-frequency digital touchpoint of a national energy retailer: inherited slow and unstable, rebuilt, and pushed past the competition.
role: Technical Product Manager, then Digital Technologies Lead (direct ownership)
context: Residential customers judge an energy supplier by the app long before they judge the tariff. The app I took over was slow, crashed constantly, and the store reviews said so. Fixing it meant rebuilding the platform underneath rather than patching features on top.
roleDetail: Technical Product Manager with direct project management responsibility from my arrival until July 2025: roadmap, backlog, release planning and acceptance across a team of around 20 FTEs, working in Scrum sprints for nearly two years.
scope: Full rebuild on an AWS microservices architecture with a new design system and feature parity. Consumption monitoring as the flagship addition, delivered jointly with the metering management team. iOS and Android release cycles, integration with billing, metering, Salesforce and payment back ends, authentication and in-app service journeys.
stakeholders: B2C marketing and customer operations, metering management, IT & Digital delivery teams, external development and QA partners, security, privacy and legal functions.
techTools: iOS, Android, AWS microservices, containers and serverless functions, REST integration layer, Salesforce, enterprise identity platform, Dynatrace for application performance monitoring, Jira, Confluence, Scrum ceremonies.
results: ~200k monthly active users, a 99% crash-free session rate and 4.6/5 on Google Play across 9.7k+ reviews. Consumption monitoring closed a two-year feature gap against competitors in nine months, coordinating the app and metering teams around a single delivery plan. Measurable effect on service: fewer inbound calls, fewer tickets and a higher store rating. The contested technical call was mine, keeping part of the platform serverless instead of containerising everything.

title: Online Customer Area
description: The web half of the self-service model, run as direct product manager alongside the app.
role: Technical Product Manager, then Digital Technologies Lead (direct ownership)
context: Every contact a customer resolves alone is a contact the call centre never receives. The online customer area is where the contractual self-service journeys live, the ones too long or too formal for a phone screen, and it has to stay consistent with the app rather than drifting into a second product.
roleDetail: Technical Product Manager with direct project management responsibility until July 2025, over a team of around five FTE, later extended to the strategic evolution of the platform.
scope: Self-service journeys covering supply data, consumption, invoices, payments, contract changes and online withdrawal. Consent and preference management, alignment with the mobile app on a shared service backbone and a single authentication model, replatforming roadmap.
stakeholders: Customer operations, B2C marketing, IT & Digital delivery, legal and privacy, external development partners.
techTools: Salesforce, billing and metering integration layer, enterprise identity platform, web analytics, Jira, Confluence.
results: High-volume service journeys progressively moved from assisted channels to self-service, contributing to the reduction in calls and tickets recorded across the B2C channels. Consent management consolidated into a single governed layer, and one authentication model shared with the app instead of two divergent ones.

title: Meter-to-Cash Programme
description: Managerial ownership of the IT & Digital portfolio behind the full chain from meter reading to cash collection, for a customer base of one million supply points.
context: In energy retail, everything between the meter and the bank account is one chain: a metering flow that fails becomes an unbilled contract, an unbilled contract becomes a credit case, and a credit case becomes churn. Managing these workstreams separately is what produces the leakage. The portfolio I inherited was run in waterfall, with priorities set project by project.
roleDetail: Digital Customer Operations Manager, accountable for the IT & Digital portfolio across the Meter-to-Cash chain: priorities, budget, vendors and delivery. Individual projects were run by dedicated project managers within the team; this is the programme layer above them.
scope: Metering and master data, billing and invoicing, credit and collections, market and switching processes, regulatory compliance, care and claims. Portfolio governance, demand intake, vendor and capacity planning, and the agile transition of the three delivery teams covering master data, billing and credit.
stakeholders: Customer operations, finance and credit, regulatory affairs, IT & Digital, distributors and market operators, BPO and technology vendors.
techTools: Salesforce, billing suite, metering and market-flow platforms, credit management system, data platform, Jira, Confluence, SAFe cadences.
results: A portfolio run as one chain rather than silos, serving one million power and gas customers, with shared master data, a common delivery cadence and a single view of regulatory deadlines across all workstreams. The three Meter-to-Cash delivery teams moved from waterfall to an agile operating model within twelve months, cutting waste and re-anchoring the backlog to the highest business priorities. Consolidated result across the applications managed over the years: a 15-25% year-over-year reduction in support tickets.

title: Technology Leadership & Governance
description: A cross-cutting mandate held in parallel with every other role: how the direction delivers, what it runs on, and what it knows.
role: Digital Technologies Lead, then Technologies Manager
context: A B2C IT & Digital direction can deliver project by project and still be ungovernable, with no shared cadence, no architectural line, no view of what is ageing underneath, and cloud spend nobody owns. On behalf of the Head of, I carried the transversal mandate that holds those threads together, alongside my product and programme responsibilities rather than instead of them.
roleDetail: Digital Technologies Lead, then Technologies Manager: governance of the agile operating model, architectural consistency, obsolescence and technical debt, and the operational link between group IT and the Italian leadership on the journey to cloud. The authority was advisory rather than hierarchical for most of it, influence earned by being right in the room, including telling the CIO that a healthy level of CloudFormation drift exists and that driving it to zero is not a realistic target.
scope: Agile operating model across twelve team rooms in the technology perimeter, Lean Portfolio Management, quarterly budget and activity planning, roadmapping, delivery traceability and control, formation of cross-functional product teams, architectural consistency reviews, obsolescence and technical debt management, ENGIE Italia cloud governance on AWS and marginally GCP, sole administration of the mobile app store consoles, group initiatives representing the Italian B2C perimeter, cloud fundamentals training and learning paths for the whole direction. Line management of the delivery teams and infrastructure engineering sat outside the mandate.
stakeholders: Head of B2C IT & Digital, group IT functions, Italian leadership, delivery teams and product owners, business counterparts, cloud and technology vendors, HR for the training programme.
techTools: AWS as primary platform and GCP, Google Play Console and App Store Connect, Jira and Confluence, SAFe and Lean Portfolio Management, CloudFormation and infrastructure-as-code practices, internal knowledge base.
results: B2C teams and collaborators moved onto a shared agile operating model, with quarterly budget and roadmap planning replacing project-by-project prioritisation and 5k+ Jira stories tracked under one delivery governance. Cross-functional product teams established, with measurably better onboarding of new joiners and a closer working relationship with the business. Cloud costs down 5-10% year over year, a collective result the governance supported. Cloud fundamentals training planned for the entire direction, with dedicated learning paths for new joiners and for specific topics such as IoT, and internal knowledge sharing reaching thousands of views.

title: Agile & SAFe Delivery
description: Adoption of scaled agile ways of working and end-to-end optimisation of the release process.
role: Digital Technologies Lead, then Digital Customer Operations Manager
context: A portfolio spanning six workstreams, several vendors and a fixed regulatory calendar cannot be planned annually. Scaling agile beyond individual squads, and shortening the release train itself, was the condition for absorbing regulatory work without freezing the commercial roadmap.
roleDetail: Driver of agile and SAFe adoption within the Italian IT & Digital organisation, and sponsor of the release-process optimisation workstream.
scope: Introduction of SAFe cadences and planning increments, backlog and refinement discipline across internal and vendor teams, role definition for product owners and delivery leads, end-to-end release process optimisation to reduce time-to-market, delivery metrics and reporting.
stakeholders: IT & Digital teams, business product owners, external delivery partners, PMO, management.
techTools: Jira, Confluence, Miro, Kanban and PI planning, DevOps toolchain, delivery dashboards.
results: Six delivery rooms moved from waterfall to agile ways of working, brought onto a single delivery cadence with refinement and planning made traceable in one tool set, and a shortened release cycle used as the lever for time-to-market rather than added capacity.

title: Vodafone Group Data Centre Operations & Lifecycle
description: Three years inside the group data centre estate of a global telecom operator: keeping 24 European sites healthy, and retiring what no longer earned its space.
organization: Vodafone Group Data Centre (via BIP Consulting)
role: PMO for Data Centre Management, and PM on individual initiatives
context: A group data centre estate is judged on two things at once: whether it keeps running, and whether it still deserves the space, power and cooling it consumes. Answering the second question is unpopular. Every rack has an owner, every building has a history, and the saving only appears once the last workload has moved.
roleDetail: PMO for the data centre management team, and project manager on individual initiatives inside it. The position gave visibility across the whole portfolio without carrying programme accountability: reporting, coordination and the initiatives I ran personally.
scope: Health monitoring of the European estate covering 3 primary, 7 secondary and 14 further sites. Rack defragmentation, consolidating load to fill racks and empty others for space and cooling efficiency. Server and full-building decommissioning, internal audits benchmarked against ANSI/TIA-942, obsolescence management of servers and components tracked in the configuration management database, improvement plans and multi-source status reporting.
stakeholders: Group infrastructure and operations teams, local markets, facility and audit functions, infrastructure vendors, programme management.
techTools: ANSI/TIA-942 and Uptime Institute benchmarks for audit, Remedy CMDB, capacity, power and cooling reporting, project and portfolio reporting, vendor coordination.
results: A Milan estate consolidated onto two buildings through a full-building decommissioning, worth 2M+ EUR per year in avoided cost. Twenty-four European sites brought under continuous health monitoring, with defragmentation freeing rack space and cooling capacity ahead of new demand. Component and server obsolescence run as a standing lifecycle process against the CMDB rather than as a series of emergencies. Left the engagement with three junior consultants reporting to me.

title: Vodafone Group Technology Innovation Center
description: Turning technology scouting into a governed pipeline: from radar entry to a productised service the group could actually adopt.
organization: Vodafone Group Data Centre (via BIP Consulting)
context: Large infrastructure organisations do not lack ideas; they lack a route from an interesting technology to a supported service someone is willing to buy internally. Without that route, scouting produces slide decks, pilots die at handover, and local markets keep solving the same problem twice.
roleDetail: Consultant in the Technology Innovation Center, working on the technology lifecycle model, the innovation radar and the cost model behind service pricing.
scope: An innovation radar tracking roughly fifty technologies across cloud, database, storage, network and security. The staged path from scouting and proof of concept through MVP, productisation and entry into the group service catalogue. Handover packages covering operating model, reference design, security agreement and training. A cost model balancing on-premise service sizes for potential chargeback to local markets, and recurring decision material for project, finance and leadership audiences.
stakeholders: Group infrastructure and architecture functions, local markets as service consumers, security, finance, vendors, operations teams receiving the handover.
techTools: Private cloud and public cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP), VMware on AWS and GCP, Kubernetes and container services, service mesh, serverless, edge computing. Storage: object storage, software-defined and unified storage, persistent storage for containers (CSI). Databases: Oracle, MS SQL on Linux, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, DBaaS. Network: SD-WAN, network infrastructure as code, load balancing as a service, IPv6 enablement, converged monitoring and telemetry. Security: host-based and cloud-native container security, software-defined firewalling, automated patch management. Cost modelling in Excel and executive reporting.
results: A documented lifecycle from radar entry to catalogue adoption, with each technology carrying its own reference design, operating model and training material at handover. The cost model I built produced a negative but decisive answer: indirect costs dominated to the point where the size of a virtual machine made almost no difference to the final figure, so size-based chargeback to local markets was not adopted. The analysis closed the question rather than leaving it open.

title: FCA France wiAdvisor Dealer Rollout
description: Digital service reception rolled out across a national dealer network, one site at a time.
context: wiAdvisor moves vehicle service reception onto a tablet, in front of the customer, at the moment the car is handed over. The technology was the easy part. The network was not: owned and independent dealerships, uneven infrastructure, and workshop staff whose relationship with a tablet ranged from indifference to throwing it across the room. Adoption, not deployment, was the real deliverable.
roleDetail: PMO and project analyst inside the ICT France organisation, working in French across the network and reporting to both French and Turin management.
scope: Tracking of the dealer sites to be activated, owned and independent. Functional and compatibility checks against local dealer management platforms, on-site testing and issue resolution, wave planning and status reporting to management on both sides.
stakeholders: Site Director, ICT France, after-sales business lines, dealer principals and workshop staff, local IT vendors, Turin headquarters.
techTools: wiAdvisor tablet application, dealer management system interfaces, site connectivity and device configuration, rollout tracking and test management, bilingual status reporting.
results: Sixty dealer sites activated in seven months, with compatibility and security validated per platform ahead of each wave. For the client the outcome was a digitalised service reception process; for the dealers, access to incentives reserved for those who adopted it. The recurring blocker was human rather than technical, and was resolved on site through configuration, hand-holding and follow-up per dealership.

title: The Way Of Life (CyberCoconut)
description: Co-founded a four-person studio and shipped a narrative game to a million downloads. Everything outside the code was mine to solve.
context: An independent studio has no distribution, no marketing budget and no second attempt. The team was a programmer, a designer and an animator. Everything else, from company paperwork to funding, game design decisions, store presence and players, had to be covered by someone, and that someone was me. The game itself is a narrative title about the choices of three characters at different ages, dealing with subjects most commercial games avoid.
roleDetail: Co-founder. Game design alongside the team, crowdfunding, administration and the commercial side of getting the title in front of players.
scope: Game design and narrative structure, the crowdfunding campaign, company administration and legal paperwork, Steam store presence and launch, localisation planning, press and community management. Engine and gameplay programming and art production belonged to the rest of the team.
stakeholders: Co-founders and the development team, crowdfunding backers, gaming press and events, the Steam player community.
techTools: Unity, Steam, Eppela crowdfunding, community and press management.
results:
One million downloads on Steam from a self-funded team of four. The Free Edition shipped on 31 May 2016 and still holds 72% positive across more than 3,800 player reviews, in five languages (English, Italian, French, German, Russian) with full English voice-over. Crowdfunding raised 10k EUR on Eppela. I answered player reviews personally from my own Steam account, and what came back from those exchanges fed into the game. A Definitive Edition followed in 2018, after my exit from the company.

title: Metering & Master Data
description: A meter-data platform and a master data management layer as the foundation of the billing chain.
context: Consumption data arrives from dozens of distributors in heterogeneous formats and at different cadences. Without a normalised meter-data layer, time-of-use tariffs cannot be priced, hourly billing cannot be produced and every distributor merger becomes a manual data-remediation exercise.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the workstream; delivery run by project managers in the team.
scope: Meter-data platform enabling time-of-use and hourly pricing, master data management implementation, alignment of supply-point and distributor master data through market consolidation, adaptation of meter-replacement flows for gas.
stakeholders: Customer operations, billing and finance, regulatory affairs, data and analytics, distributors and market operators, platform vendors.
techTools: Meter data management platform, market-flow integration, MDM tooling, data warehouse and lakehouse, Salesforce and billing integration.
results: Consumption data normalised into a single governed layer, enabling consumption-based tariff families downstream and absorbing distributor consolidation without breaking the supply-point base.

title: Billing & Invoicing
description: Bill redesign, hourly billing and the replatforming of the customer communication engine.
context: The bill is the document a customer reads most often and the one that generates most inbound contacts. At the same time, new consumption-based tariffs required the billing engine to move from monthly aggregates to hourly granularity, and the output-management platform behind every customer document had reached end of life.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the workstream; delivery run by project managers in the team.
scope: Redesign of the customer bill, hourly billing capability, replatforming of the document composition and output management stack, excise-duty rate handling across residential and business gas supplies.
stakeholders: Customer operations, finance and tax, regulatory affairs, marketing and communication, IT & Digital delivery, document platform vendor.
techTools: Billing suite, document composition and output management platform, archive and delivery channels, Salesforce, metering integration layer.
results: A redesigned bill aligned with regulatory transparency requirements, billing capable of hourly granularity for consumption-based products, and customer document production moved onto a supported platform.

title: Credit & Collections
description: Credit management platform renewal, payment-method shift and automation of the collections cycle.
context: Days sales outstanding in energy retail is driven less by customer willingness to pay than by the quality of the collections chain: how fast a missed payment is detected, how it is dunned, when suspension is triggered and how easily a customer can regularise. Legacy tooling made each of those steps slow and manual.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the workstream; delivery run by project managers in the team.
scope: Scouting and implementation of a credit management system, evolution of power and gas suspension processes, credit-scoring framework at contract subscription for small-business customers, shift of the base towards direct debit and electronic billing at acquisition, instalment plans for eligible customers, automation of foreign IBAN and foreign bank handling.
stakeholders: Credit and finance, customer operations, sales, legal, IT & Digital delivery, collections BPO and platform vendors.
techTools: Credit management system, Salesforce, billing suite, payment and direct-debit gateways, credit bureau interfaces, workflow automation.
results: A modernised credit chain: risk assessed at subscription rather than after the first unpaid bill, dunning and suspension automated, and payment methods steered towards direct debit at the point of acquisition.

title: Regulatory Compliance Delivery
description: Turning a continuous stream of energy-authority resolutions into delivered IT changes, on fixed legal deadlines.
context: An energy retailer does not choose its regulatory backlog or its dates. Each resolution from the national authority lands as a hard deadline that cuts across contracts, billing, products, communications and market flows at the same time, and non-compliance is measured in sanctions, not in delayed features.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the regulatory delivery portfolio: impact assessment, prioritisation against the commercial roadmap, and deadline governance.
scope: Contract and renewal compliance, transparency and quality-of-service requirements, product and general-conditions adaptations, customer migration obligations, indemnity handling, certified electronic delivery, electricity market-design measures, compliant offer publication to the central market system, digitalisation of the underlying processes.
stakeholders: Regulatory affairs, legal, customer operations, marketing and product, finance, IT & Digital delivery, external counsel and system integrators.
techTools: Salesforce, billing suite, contract and document management, market-flow platform, workflow automation, portfolio and deadline tracking.
results: A recurring compliance stream absorbed without disrupting the commercial roadmap, with impacts assessed once and delivered across all affected systems, and process digitalisation used to lower the cost of each subsequent regulatory wave.

title: Customer Care, Claims & Feedback
description: Closing the loop between what customers say and what the organisation changes, and automating the regulated part of it.
role: Digital Technologies Lead (survey), then customer operations perimeter (claims, after-sales)
period: 08/2025 – 09/2026 (claims and after-sales); survey delivered in the previous role
context: Most companies collect feedback and few act on it. The gap is structural: satisfaction data sits in one system, claims in another, and no process converts either into a backlog item with a named owner. Claims handling in particular, regulated and deadline-bound, was still largely manual case work.
roleDetail: Two distinct contributions in two roles: implementation of the customer survey and its feedback process, delivered as Digital Technologies Lead; then claims and after-sales automation under the customer operations perimeter.
scope: Design and implementation of the customer survey and the process routing its output to named owners, claims automation across two delivery waves, after-sales service model for the retail and door-to-door channels. Speech analytics and public review management belong to the same feedback programme but were run outside this contribution.
stakeholders: Customer operations and contact centre, quality, marketing and communication, regulatory affairs, IT & Digital delivery, BPO partners.
techTools: Salesforce Marketing Cloud for customer communications and survey delivery, Salesforce case management, workflow automation, reporting.
results: A survey process with defined ownership of the resulting actions rather than a score reported and filed, and claims handling moved from manual case work to automated workflows.

title: Data Platform & Analytics
description: Customer intelligence built on a governed lakehouse rather than on channel-local reporting.
context: Digital behaviour was recorded per touchpoint, commercial performance per channel and value per contract. Nothing joined them, so segmentation, lifetime value and adaptive offering all stalled at the point where the data had to be combined.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the customer-data and analytics workstream in customer operations.
scope: Porting of digital behavioural data into the enterprise data platform and BI layer, customer intelligence and adaptive-offering model, customer lifetime value construction, analytical foundations for segmentation and next-best-offer.
stakeholders: Data and analytics, marketing and CRM, sales, finance, IT & Digital delivery, privacy, platform vendors.
techTools: Lakehouse and data platform, BI and self-service reporting, customer data model, segmentation and scoring models, Salesforce Marketing Cloud integration.
results: Digital behaviour, commercial and contractual data joined in one platform, with lifetime value and customer intelligence available as inputs to campaigns, pricing and service decisions instead of as one-off analyses.

title: Cloud Operations & DevOps
description: Cloud migration, DevOps adoption and disciplined application lifecycle management across the digital estate.
context: Digital touchpoints accumulate platforms faster than they retire them. Without an explicit lifecycle of migrate, upgrade and decommission, the estate grows in cost and in unpatched surface, and every new feature is delivered on top of technical debt someone else deferred.
roleDetail: Manager of cloud operations across the B2C digital products, alongside product ownership of the touchpoints themselves.
scope: End-to-end technological upgrades, migration of digital workloads to cloud platforms, DevOps adoption in the delivery chain, application lifecycle management and decommissioning of superseded platforms.
stakeholders: IT infrastructure and cloud, cyber security, IT & Digital delivery teams, application vendors, procurement.
techTools: AWS, Google Cloud Platform, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, monitoring and observability, CMDB and lifecycle tracking.
results: Digital workloads moved onto cloud platforms with delivery automated through CI/CD, and superseded applications actively decommissioned rather than left running, keeping the estate's cost and attack surface tied to what is genuinely in use.

title: ERP Modernisation AS400 to Dynamics 365
description: Switching off AS/400 at two Italian manufacturers, and translating what the business actually did into requirements a system integrator could build.
context: A legacy AS/400 that has run a manufacturer for decades is not documented anywhere except in the habits of the people using it. Replacing it with Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations means rebuilding that knowledge as explicit process and data definitions first, including product coding, which is where most of the ambiguity hides.
roleDetail: Technology expert on both engagements: the technical side of requirements, product and data coding, and the interface with the system integrator.
scope: Process mapping and technical requirements for the migration off AS/400, product coding and data model definition, technical liaison with the system integrator, decision and status material for client management, coordination of security testing activities, and hands-on enablement of client staff, down to the difference between a spreadsheet and a database. Development and the testing phase were outside the mandate: testing started after my handover.
stakeholders: C-levels, client operations, production and finance functions, client IT, the system integrator, management sponsors.
techTools: IBM AS/400 legacy landscape, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations, process and data modelling, product coding standards, requirements documentation.
results: Twenty-four processes migrated in scope at one client and thirty-six at the other, defined to the level of detail the integrator could build against, with product coding rationalised as part of the move. Handed over before the test phase.

title: AWS Cloud Training
description: Teaching cloud fundamentals to roughly a hundred people, in parallel with a full-time corporate role.
organization: Freelance instructor, with Tree Srl as training partner
role: Cloud instructor, foundational and practitioner level
context: Cloud adoption stalls on people rather than on platforms. Organisations buy the capability and then discover that the teams meant to use it have never designed for elasticity, shared responsibility or cost as an architectural constraint. Foundational training is where that gap actually closes.
roleDetail: Cloud instructor on an occasional-performance contract, delivering courses through the training partner Tree Srl alongside my day job.
scope: Four foundational and practitioner-level classes covering cloud concepts, core AWS services, security and shared responsibility, and cost design. Certification preparation at that level, and adaptation of the material to mixed corporate and early-career audiences. Course authoring, accreditation content ownership and advanced architecture tracks were not part of the mandate.
stakeholders: Training partner, corporate clients and their IT teams, individual professionals and students.
techTools:
AWS, foundational and practitioner curriculum, hands-on labs, virtual and classroom delivery.

Certification
AWS Certified Solutions Architect, Associate. AWS Authorised Instructor.
results: Around one hundred people taught the fundamentals of cloud across four classes in roughly eighteen months. The same enablement instinct was later applied inside ENGIE, where I built and planned cloud training and learning paths for all IT colleagues.

title: Switching & Market Processes (ON HOLD)
description: Faster, more reliable supplier switching, transfers of supply and activations.
context: Switching is where an energy retailer wins or loses a customer before the relationship even starts. Regulation compressed switching windows to 24 hours, while rejected requests, failed pre-checks and manual transfer-of-supply handling were leaving contracts stuck between two suppliers.
roleDetail: Manager accountable for the workstream; delivery run by project managers in the team.
scope: 24-hour switching for power and gas, pre-check redesign and repositioning within the sales journey, gas pre-check specification, transfer of supply with change of supplier across back end and front end, web transfer-with-switch journey, electrical activation process, resolution of rejected market flows and restoration cases, status tracking exposed in app and customer area.
stakeholders: Customer operations, sales channels, regulatory affairs, IT & Digital delivery, distributors and the central market information system, BPO partners.
techTools: Market-flow integration platform, Salesforce, billing and metering systems, workflow orchestration, customer-facing status APIs.
results: Switching and transfer processes aligned with compressed regulatory timelines, rejection cases handled through automated remediation flows, and customers able to follow the state of their request in the digital channels.

title: weRank
description: A fantasy league for competitive League of Legends, built on Riot's public match data. We had the data and we had the formulas, and never got to run one against the other.
context: Fantasy sports work because performance is public, structured, and scored the same way for everyone. Esports produces more raw data than any traditional sport and Riot Games publishes a large part of it through a public API, but there is no agreed way to turn a match record into a player's score. A player's contribution to a win is spread across kills and assists, objectives, vision control, gold efficiency and tempo, and none of those is a fantasy point on its own. The bet was that the scoring model, not the app around it, was the hard and defensible part.
roleDetail: Gaming domain expert among four friends building it after hours. I was the one who played and followed competitive League of Legends, so my job was to say what actually counts in a match: which of the dozens of statistics the API exposes reflect a player's contribution to a win, and which are noise that looks like signal. The scoring formulas were built on that judgement.
scope: Riot's public API as the only data source, with no scraping and no private feeds. Bulk collection of match and player statistics, definition of the player KPIs, and the aggregation formulas converting a match record into a comparable performance value. Product concept and the rules of the game around it.
stakeholders: The four founders, and the competitive League of Legends player base as the intended audience.
techTools: Riot Games public API, bulk match and player statistics, scoring model design.
results:
Several gigabytes of match data collected, and the aggregation formulas defined. The two were never brought together: the step from raw data to a running score is exactly where the venture stopped. The development lead became a father, his spare time went to zero, and with four friends working on it in the evenings there was no way to replace him without starting over. We closed it rather than keep a project alive that existed only on paper.

The failure was neither technical nor conceptual. Both halves were there and nobody had the capacity to close the last mile. It is the same pattern worth watching at work: a delivery is not at risk when the design is hard, it is at risk when one person holds the only route to production.
